## Learning Objectives

By the end of this presentation, you will be able to:

- Understand the role of liver resection for HCC in cirrhotic patients
- Apply **Makuuchi's criteria** for determining surgical indications
- Describe perioperative management of cirrhosis and portal hypertension
- Explain key surgical techniques: inflow occlusion, IOUS, anatomic resection
- Compare surgical devices for liver parenchyma division
- Discuss laparoscopic approaches and advanced maneuvers

# (Section divider handled by slide titles below)

## Introduction — Local Tumor Control

- **Local tumor control** is the most important consideration in treating hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
- HCC is the most common diagnosis associated with hepatic resection in the setting of **cirrhosis**
- Liver resection can **completely remove cancerous tissues**
- Theoretically regarded as a **curative treatment** for HCC

## The Cirrhotic Liver — A Dual Problem

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Patients with HCC often have **injured liver tissue or cirrhosis**
- This factor must be considered when deciding therapeutic strategy
- Two competing priorities:
  1. Complete tumor removal
  2. Preservation of liver function
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.callout-note}
## Figure 120.1 — Appearance of the Cirrhotic Liver
**(A)** Gross appearance of the cirrhotic liver — nodular surface
**(B)** Cut surface — regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa
:::
:::
:::

## Liver Transplantation — The Ideal Treatment

- Liver transplantation is an **ideal treatment for early-stage HCC**
- Especially for lesions meeting:
  - **Milan criteria**, and/or
  - Other expanded criteria for liver transplantation

**Why transplantation is attractive:**

- Removes **all injured liver tissues** with potential for carcinogenesis
- Removes the **existing HCC** simultaneously

## The Graft Shortage Problem

- A **severe graft shortage** limits transplantation
- Hepatic surgeons are sometimes forced to select **liver resection as a first-line therapeutic strategy** for HCC rather than transplantation
- The **safety of liver resection** has been established:
  - Present mortality rate: **2%–5%**
  - Even in patients with **liver cirrhosis**

## Second Priority — Preserving Liver Function

- **Prevention of further deterioration in liver function** is the second priority in HCC treatment
- Liver resection can be associated with **significant blood loss**
- Remains **technically demanding**

**To prevent fatal complications (e.g., liver failure):**

- Careful **patient selection**
- Meticulous **perioperative management**

## Avoiding Excessive Resection

- Extensive removal of **noncancerous liver parenchyma should be avoided** as much as possible
- Accurate evaluation of:
  - Liver volume **to be removed**
  - Liver volume **to be preserved**
- This is critical when deciding on an appropriate procedure

## Scope of This Chapter

General aspects of liver resection for HCC in patients with cirrhosis:

| Domain | Focus |
|---|---|
| Surgical indication | Liver function, tumor factors, portal hypertension |
| Perioperative management | Diuretics, portal hypertension management |
| **Surgical techniques** | **Special emphasis of this chapter** |

## Surgical Indication — Three Pillars

Surgical indication for hepatectomy in cirrhotic patients rests on assessment of:

1. **Liver functional reserve**
2. **Tumor-related factors**
3. **Portal hypertension**

---

## Liver Functional Reserve — ICG R15

- In **Eastern countries**, the **indocyanine green retention rate at 15 minutes (ICG R15)** is regarded as an important tool
- Used for accurately assessing **what liver volume to remove**
- Especially in **Japan**, criteria consisting of:
  - ICG R15 value
  - Ascites
  - Jaundice

...known as **"Makuuchi's criteria"** — widely used for decisions on surgical indications and to estimate tolerable resection volumes in cirrhotic patients

## Makuuchi's Criteria — Absolute Contraindications

**Liver resection is absolutely contraindicated when:**

- **Uncontrollable ascites** even after use of diuretics, AND/OR
- Serum total bilirubin level **constantly higher than 2.0 mg/dL**

## Makuuchi's Criteria — Mildly Elevated Bilirubin

When serum total bilirubin level is **1.1–1.9 mg/dL**:

- Only **tumor enucleation** or
- **Resection of a small part of the liver** is possible

When serum total bilirubin level is **≤ 1.0 mg/dL**:

- The surgical procedure can be determined based on the **ICG R15 value**

## ICG R15-Based Decision — Normal Liver

If ICG R15 is **normal (< 10%)**:

- A **major hepatectomy** may be feasible, including:
  - Right hemihepatectomy
  - Left trisegmentectomy
  - Central bisegmentectomy

## ICG R15 — Slightly Injured Liver (10%–19%)

If ICG R15 is **10%–19%**:

- A **one-third resection** can be performed:
  - Left hemihepatectomy, OR
  - Right lateral sectionectomy, OR
  - Paramedian sectionectomy
- **Major hepatectomy would be associated with high risk**

## ICG R15 — Moderately Injured Liver (20%–29%)

If ICG R15 is **20%–29%**:

- A **one-sixth resection** is possible, corresponding to:
  - A **left lateral section**, OR
  - **One Couinaud segment**

## ICG R15 — Severely Injured Liver (> 30%)

If ICG R15 is **more than 30%**:

- Only a **limited resection** can be considered

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Principle
As liver function deteriorates (rising ICG R15), the tolerable resection volume shrinks progressively: major hepatectomy → one-third → one-sixth → limited resection.
:::

## Summary Table — Makuuchi's Criteria

| Ascites | Total Bilirubin | ICG R15 | Allowable Resection |
|---|---|---|---|
| Not controlled | Any | Any | **Not indicated for hepatectomy** |
| None / controlled | ≥ 2.0 mg/dL | — | **Not indicated for hepatectomy** |
| None / controlled | 1.6–1.9 mg/dL | — | Enucleation |
| None / controlled | 1.1–1.5 mg/dL | — | Enucleation / limited |
| None / controlled | ≤ 1.0 mg/dL | Normal (< 10%) | Major hepatectomy (trisectoriectomy, bisectoriectomy, left hepatectomy) |
| None / controlled | ≤ 1.0 mg/dL | 10%–19% | Monosectoriectomy (segmentectomy) |
| None / controlled | ≤ 1.0 mg/dL | 20%–29% | Limited resection / enucleation |
| None / controlled | ≤ 1.0 mg/dL | 30%–39% | Limited resection / enucleation |
| None / controlled | ≤ 1.0 mg/dL | ≥ 40% | Limited resection / enucleation |

*(Recreated from Figure 120.2 decision tree; note: "sectionectomy" is now preferred for tri-, bi-, mono-sectionectomy.)*

## Figure 120.2 — Decision Tree for Operative Procedures

::: {.callout-note}
## Makuuchi's Decision Tree (Makuuchi M, Kosuge T, Takayama T, et al. Semin Surg Oncol. 1993;9:298–304)
**Step 1:** Ascites → Not controlled = **No hepatectomy**
**Step 2:** Total bilirubin:
 - ≥ 2.0 mg/dL → Not indicated
 - 1.6–1.9 mg/dL → Enucleation
 - 1.1–1.5 mg/dL → Enucleation (K values 0.15/0.11/0.08/0.06 guide safe resection rate)
 - Normal → proceed to ICG R15
**Step 3:** ICG R15:
 - < 10% → Trisectoriectomy / bisectoriectomy / left hepatectomy
 - 10%–19% → Monosectoriectomy / segmentectomy
 - 20%–29% → Limited resection
 - ≥ 30% → Enucleation / limited resection
:::

## Validation of Makuuchi's Criteria — Torzilli et al.

- Torzilli and colleagues applied the criteria to **107 consecutive patients** (59.8% cirrhosis) undergoing liver resection for HCC

**Results:**

| Outcome | Rate |
|---|---|
| Mortality | **0%** |
| Morbidity | **26.2%** |

## ICG R15 as a Predictor of Mortality

- A study of **127 patients with HCC** investigated the relationship between preoperative liver function and postoperative complications
- The **ICG R15 value was confirmed to be the most significant factor** for prediction of mortality

**Recent refinements:**

- Refined and expanded Makuuchi's criteria have been proposed
- Incorporate the **accurate estimation of remnant liver volume**

---

## Tumor-Related Factors — Single and Small HCC

- In general, a **single and small HCC** is a **good indication for resection**

## Tumor-Related Factors — Multifocal and Large Lesions

- **Multifocal and large lesions** can also be treated by resection
- Provides **satisfactory long-term outcomes**

## Advanced HCC with Vascular Invasion

- Liver resection can offer **acceptable results** for advanced HCC with vascular invasion
- Compared with the use of a **molecular targeted agent (Sorafenib)**
- Sorafenib is recommended in the treatment algorithm of the **Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) group**

## The BCLC Controversy

- The BCLC algorithm is considered the **treatment standard worldwide**
- However, **several investigators have objected** to this algorithm
- Especially regarding the **extent of restrictions placed on surgical indications**
- Consequently, **several additional treatment algorithms** are now available (e.g., APASL, HKLC, JSH guidelines)

---

## Portal Hypertension — Definition and Diagnosis

- Usually defined as a **hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) ≥ 10 mm Hg**
- Can be **practically diagnosed** by the presence of:
  - **Esophageal varices**, AND/OR
  - **Platelet count < 100,000/mL** in association with **splenomegaly**

## Portal Hypertension — The Bruix Report (1996)

- Bruix and colleagues reported that liver resection for HCC in patients with portal hypertension led to:
  - A **high incidence of postoperative liver decompensation of as much as 73%**
- Their group later published a **meta-analysis** comparing prognosis after hepatectomy **with and without portal hypertension**
- Conclusion: portal hypertension **increases the risk for mortality and clinical decompensation** after surgery for HCC

## Guideline Position on Portal Hypertension

- Based on these results:
  - **American** and **European** guidelines for HCC management suggested that the presence of portal hypertension **may be a contraindication for liver resection**
- This recommendation is now **widely accepted worldwide**

## Counter-Evidence — Satisfactory Outcomes

- Indeed, prognosis for patients **with** portal hypertension after hepatectomy is considered relatively **poor** compared with those **without** portal hypertension
- However, **several investigators have reported satisfactory long-term outcomes** after hepatectomy for patients with portal hypertension **who were not eligible for liver transplantation**

## Rethinking Surgical Indications with Portal Hypertension

- Comparable outcomes are **difficult to obtain with other nonsurgical treatments**
- Surgical indications for HCC associated with portal hypertension **should be discussed further**

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Correct Comparison
The discussion should be based NOT on:
- Comparison **with vs. without portal hypertension** among hepatectomy patients

But rather on:
- Comparison **with vs. without surgical treatment** among patients who **have** portal hypertension
:::

## Implication for BCLC Guidelines

- Consequently, the **BCLC guidelines may need to be modified** in terms of the role of surgery

---

## Perioperative Management — Overview

Key perioperative issues in cirrhotic patients:

1. **Diuretics** — preventing refractory ascites and edema
2. **Management for portal hypertension** — varices, thrombocytopenia

## Diuretics — Spironolactone

- **Routine administration of spironolactone** (aldosterone inhibitor) is recommended
- Especially in cirrhotic patients
- Rationale: **secondary hyperaldosteronemia** is caused by low degradation of aldosterone through **liver metabolic dysfunction**

## Spironolactone Dosing by ICG R15

| ICG R15 | Spironolactone Dose |
|---|---|
| < 20% | **100 mg/day** |
| > 20% | **200 mg/day** |

**If ascites is uncontrollable:**

- Administration of **furosemide** is a better choice
- Initial dose of **10 or 20 mg/day**

---

## Management for Portal Hypertension — Preoperative Evaluation

If liver resection is scheduled in a patient with portal hypertension:

- **Careful preoperative evaluation and management are mandatory**
- **Gastrointestinal endoscopy** is necessary to evaluate the presence or absence of:
  - **Esophageal varices**
  - **Gastric varices**
- These are frequently associated with liver cirrhosis

## Esophageal Varices — Preoperative Treatment

- If found, esophageal varices with a **high risk of rupture** (e.g., those with a **red color sign**) should be treated **before surgery** using:
  - **Endoscopic ligation**, OR
  - **Sclerotherapy**

## Gastric Varices — Hassab's Operation

- **Hassab's operation** should be considered for gastric varices with a high risk of rupture
- Procedure: **devascularization around the upper stomach with a splenectomy**

## Thrombocytopenia and Splenectomy

- **Thrombocytopenia** (platelet count < 50,000/mL) caused by **hypersplenism** is a major symptom of portal hypertension
- A **splenectomy is recommended before liver resection** to reduce the risks of:
  - **Intraoperative blood loss**
  - **Postoperative liver failure**

## Figure 120.3 — Strategies for Perioperative Prophylactic Management (PPM)

::: {.callout-note}
## PPM Decision Algorithm (Takemura N, et al. Br J Surg. 2019;106(8):1066–1074)
**Starting point:** Patients with HCC & portal hypertension (PH)

**Branch by platelet count:**

- **Platelets ≥ 5.0 × 10⁴/μL** → assess varices:
  - No varix or ≤ F1 → **Hepatectomy without PPM**
  - Esophagus varix ≥ F2,3, RC(+) → **EVL or EIS**
  - Stomach varix ≥ F2,3, RC(+) → **BRTO** (indicated since 1999)
  - Esophagus & stomach varices → **EVL & BRTO**
- **Platelets < 5.0 × 10⁴/μL** → **Splenectomy**, with possible additions:
  - Varix (esophagus) → Splenectomy + EVL/EIS
  - Varix (stomach) → Splenectomy + BRTO or **Hassab**

*On occasion, EVL + splenectomy or BRTO + splenectomy could be performed.*
*BRTO = balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration; EIS = endoscopic injection sclerotherapy; EVL = endoscopic variceal ligation.*
:::

## Surgical Techniques — Overview

Techniques covered in this chapter:

1. Inflow and outflow occlusion
2. Intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS)
3. Anatomic resection
4. Laparoscopic liver resection
5. Surgical devices for parenchyma division
6. Anterior approach and hanging maneuver
7. Hepatic vein reconstruction

---

## Inflow and Outflow Occlusion — Historical Context

- **Ischemia-reperfusion injury** was once viewed as a critical form of damage to the liver
- Neither inflow nor outflow occlusion was applied during liver parenchymal division
- Result: liver resection was inevitably associated with **large blood loss**
- This sometimes led to **liver failure and death**

## Evolution of Vascular Occlusion

- **Early 1980s:** the **hemihepatic vascular occlusion method** was devised
- The **total inflow occlusion (Pringle maneuver)** became widely used
- These inflow occlusion methods contributed to a **marked reduction in blood loss**
- The usefulness of the Pringle maneuver was confirmed by a **randomized controlled trial (RCT) performed in Hong Kong**

## Total Vascular Exclusion

- **Total vascular exclusion** was performed for a time
- However, due to:
  - The **complexity of the procedure**, and
  - The **risk of postoperative liver dysfunction**
- It is now **used infrequently**

## Ischemic Preconditioning and Intermittent Occlusion

- Clavien and colleagues found that **10 minutes of ischemic preconditioning** by inflow occlusion **significantly improved postoperative liver function**
- The **superiority of intermittent inflow occlusion** versus continuous or total occlusion is now **widely accepted**
- This is an **indispensable technique** for improving the safety of liver surgery

---

## Intraoperative Ultrasound (IOUS) — Introduction

- IOUS was **first introduced in the field of liver surgery in the late 1970s by Makuuchi**
- Enables liver surgeons to grasp:
  - The **location of tumors**
  - **Anatomic structures**

## Impact of IOUS on Safety

- Using IOUS, the **safety of liver resection has been remarkably improved**
- Especially in patients with **cirrhosis**, because:
  - A **limited resection** to minimize loss of liver parenchyma is possible under IOUS guidance
- IOUS is also useful for the **detection of occult HCCs** that cannot be detected using preoperative imaging modalities

## Contrast-Enhanced IOUS

- Detection ability has been further improved by using **contrast media**, such as:
  - **Perfluorobutane microbubbles (Sonazoid)**

::: {.callout-important}
## Bottom Line
**IOUS will continue to be indispensable for liver surgery.**
:::

---

## Anatomic Resection — Rationale

HCC has a unique biologic characteristic:

- It tends to **spread intrahepatically**
- It **metastasizes through the portal venous system**
- Even a small HCC may be associated with **portal venous invasion**, which correlates with **worse prognosis**
- Surgeons should consider **removing potential intrahepatic metastases** whenever possible

## Anatomic Resection — Balancing Risks

**The dilemma in cirrhotic liver:**

- **Major hepatic resection should be avoided** because of the high risk of postoperative critical liver failure

**The solution:**

- **Anatomic resection** — the entire segment fed by the tumor-bearing portal branches is **completely and systematically removed**
- A reasonable surgical procedure for **preventing recurrence via the portal venous pathway**

## Anatomic Subsegmentectomy — Origin

- Anatomic subsegmentectomy was **first proposed by Makuuchi and colleagues**
- Depending on the size and location of the tumor, the following can be performed:
  - Resection of a **complete Couinaud segment**
  - **Part of a segment**
  - **More than one segment** extending to the adjacent region

## Figure 120.4 — Procedures for Anatomic Resection of HCC

::: {.callout-note}
## Technique (Makuuchi M, Hasegawa H, Yamazaki S. Surg Gynecol Obstet. 1986;161:346–350)
1. A **blue dye (indigo carmine)** is injected into the **portal venous branch bearing the tumor** under IOUS guidance
2. From the liver surface, a portal branch is **manually punctured distal to the point of ligation**
3. The **stained surface of the liver is marked** with electric cautery
4. **Parenchymal dissection** follows the marked line
5. The **hepatic veins should be exposed longitudinally** on the dissected surface after complete resection
:::

## Figure 120.5 — Dissected Surface After Segment VIII Resection

::: {.callout-note}
## Complete SVIII Resection
- Dissected surface after complete resection of liver **segment VIII (SVIII)**
- Key exposed structures:
  - **MHV** (middle hepatic vein)
  - **RHV** (right hepatic vein)
  - **P8 ventral stump** and **P8 dorsal stump** (portal vein branches of SVIII)
- Hepatic veins exposed longitudinally confirm a true anatomic resection
*(Kishi Y, et al. Br J Surg. 2012;99(8):1105–1112)*
:::

## ICG as an Alternative Staining Material

- **ICG** is another useful staining material that can be used instead of indigo carmine
- ICG is illuminated by **near-infrared light** and emits fluorescence
- Peak wavelength: **about 840 nm**
- This lies within the range of absorbance spectra of:
  - Hemoglobin (< 600 nm)
  - Water (> 900 nm)

## ICG Fluorescence Imaging System

- The wavelength of ICG excited by near-infrared light is **not visible to the human eye**
- Therefore, the **ICG fluorescence system equipped with interferential filters** is applied to obtain fluorescence images

## Figure 120.6 — ICG Fluorescent Anatomical Hepatectomy

::: {.callout-note}
## ICG Fluorescence-Guided Resection
- Near-infrared fluorescence imaging reveals the boundary between:
  - The **ICG-stained (positive) segment** to be resected
  - The **unstained (negative) remnant liver**
- Allows real-time visualization of segmental boundaries during parenchymal transection
- Applicable to both open and **laparoscopic hepatectomy**
:::

## Technical Difficulty of Anatomic Resection

- Anatomic subsegmentectomy is **technically difficult to perform**, especially for:
  - **Segments IV, VII, and VIII**
- Reasons:
  - These locations are **surrounded by major vascular structures**
  - They do not necessarily present with a **flat dissection plane**

## Evidence — Anatomic vs. Nonanatomic Resection

- To date, **several studies have shown that anatomic resection is superior** to nonanatomic resection

::: {.callout-tip}
## Recommendation
As long as liver function is adequate, **anatomic resection is strongly recommended** as the surgical procedure of choice for HCC.
:::

- Anatomic hepatic resection has been recently applied in **laparoscopic hepatectomy**

---

## Laparoscopic Liver Resection — Introduction

- Laparoscopy currently plays a **major role** in abdominal surgery
- Enables **minimally invasive procedures**
- Laparoscopic liver resection for HCC was **initially applied as a treatment option for peripheral HCC**

## Louisville Consensus Statement (2008)

- **45 experts** proposed that the most suitable candidates among HCC patients for laparoscopic liver resection are those with:
  - **Solitary lesions**
  - Measuring **≤ 5 cm** in diameter
  - Located in **peripheral segments**

## Morioka Consensus Conference (2014)

The second consensus conference concluded:

| Procedure | Status |
|---|---|
| **Minor laparoscopic resection** | **Standard practice** |
| **Major laparoscopic resection** | Still considered **innovative / exploration phase** |

## Expanding Indications for Laparoscopic Resection

Recently, the indication for laparoscopic liver resection has been expanded to:

- **Limited resection** for tumors in the **deep part of the liver parenchyma**
- **Major hepatectomy**

## Why Laparoscopy Is Especially Useful in Cirrhosis

Laparoscopic resection may be **more useful for HCC, especially in cirrhotic patients**, because of:

- **Smaller destruction of the abdominal wall**
- **Lesser need for liver mobilization**
- **Lower demand for IV fluid replacement** (minimization of unnecessary fluid loss)

## Additional Benefits of Laparoscopy in Cirrhosis

- **Fluid accumulation in the third space is also likely to be reduced**
- Results in:
  - **Decreased risk of prolonged postoperative ascites**
  - **Shorter hospital stay**

---

## Surgical Devices for Parenchyma Division — Overview

Liver parenchyma division consists of **two procedures**:

1. **Crushing** of the liver parenchyma to detect vessels
2. **Subsequent occlusion** of those vessels

Various devices have been developed for one or both procedures. Through the introduction of inflow occlusion, refined operative techniques, and surgical devices, **blood loss has been significantly reduced**, improving the safety of liver resections.

## Clamp Crushing — The Standard

- **Clamp crushing with forceps combined with ligation remains the standard**
- Advantages:
  - **Simple**
  - **Inexpensive**
  - **Useful**

## Clamp Crushing — Technique

- Originally, the **surgeon's fingers** were used to crush liver parenchyma
- **Pean forceps** are now used
- The surgeon:
  1. Removes parenchyma with forceps
  2. Identifies vessels (**Glisson triads, hepatic vein**) by feeling structures through the tip
  3. Ligates identified vessels with a string and divides them
- **Advantage:** avoids tissue injury
- **Limitation:** experience is needed to make the fullest use of this method

## Figure 120.7 — Pean Forceps for Normal vs. Cirrhotic Liver

::: {.callout-note}
## Forceps Selection
**Normal liver parenchymal crushing:**
- **Blunt-tip** Pean forceps
- Wider opening

**Cirrhotic hard liver parenchymal crushing:**
- Relatively **thin-tip** Pean forceps
- **Not opened too much**
- In cirrhosis, liver parenchyma is **hard**, so thin tips make crushing easier
:::

## Ultrasonic Dissector — CUSA

- The **Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator (CUSA)** is a device used to:
  - **Crush** the liver parenchyma
  - **Remove crushed tissues**
  - **Expose fibrous tissues** (Glisson triads, hepatic vein)
- Works via **ultrasonic vibration at its tip**

## CUSA — Operation and Modifications

- Vessels must be exposed so they can be occluded with **ligation or sealing**, as with conventional clamp crushing
- Simultaneously, the ultrasonic dissector:
  - Supplies **saline from the tip** to wash the surgical field
  - Aspirates fluid through the tip to **maintain an adequate field of vision**
- **Modified versions** can be attached to an electrocautery device or ultrasonic scalpel

## CUSA in Cirrhotic Liver

- For division of **cirrhotic liver**:
  - The **vibration width of the tip must be set wider**
  - This can make it **more difficult to separate vessels**
  - Thin vessels are **more easily injured** than in normal liver tissue
- The CUSA has become one of the **standard surgical devices** for liver parenchyma transection

## Vessel-Sealing System — Mechanism

- Uses **bipolar electrothermal energy**
- Can seal the vessel wall by **denaturing the collagen and elastin** in the wall
- **Completely occludes** the blood vessel
- During parenchymal division, it can easily occlude vessels exposed by:
  - Clamp crushing, OR
  - An ultrasonic dissector

## Vessel-Sealing System — Benefits and Evolution

**Benefits:**

- Shortens **liver transection time**
- Reduces the **amount of blood loss**

**Evolution:**

- Improved energy generator → **stronger sealing power** while minimizing damage to adjacent tissues
- Increased sealing **speed and certainty**
- Current type: **thinner and shorter tip**
- **Built-in scissors** enable vessels to be cut immediately after sealing

## Vessel-Sealing — Practical Note

- Although clamp crushing itself is possible with the tip of the vessel-sealing system:
  - **Pean forceps enable a better feel and vessel exposure** (per the authors' experience)

## Automatic Suture Device — Vascular Stapler

- For **laparoscopic liver resection**, an automatic suture device is now an **indispensable tool**
- Frequently used to cut:
  - **Glisson triads**
  - **Hepatic veins**
- A vascular stapler was **first applied to resect hepatic veins during hepatectomy**

## Glissonean Approach with Stapler

- Figueras et al. applied this device to cut the **Glisson pedicle** with the **Glissonean approach**

::: {.callout-warning}
## Caution
When using a stapler to cut the Glisson triads, attention should be paid to **avoid accidental injury of the bile duct confluence**. The Glisson triads should be cut with the stapler **on the peripheral side as far as possible**.
:::

## Stapler Hepatectomy

- Some surgeons apply the vascular stapler for **liver parenchymal resection** — called **"stapler hepatectomy"**
- **Advantage:** may reduce parenchymal transection time
- **Risk:** **hepatic vein avulsion injury**, especially in patients with cirrhosis
  - Hemostasis even from thin hepatic veins is sometimes **difficult**

---

## Anterior Approach vs. Conventional Approach

**Conventional approach:**

- Before parenchyma transection, the liver is **mobilized** (e.g., in right hepatectomy, the right hemiliver is fully mobilized from the right adrenal gland, with extrahepatic division of the right hepatic vein)
- Enables the surgeon to **control bleeding easily**
- **Thoracophrenolaparotomy** is a good option to safely complete mobilization of the right liver

## Rationale for the Anterior Approach

- Several surgeons recommend the **anterior approach**: liver parenchyma division is done **before mobilization**, especially when the tumor is **large**
- Believed to avoid the risks of:
  - **Massive bleeding** from hepatic vein avulsion
  - **Prolonged ischemia** in the remnant liver
  - **Spillage of cancer cells** into the systemic circulation

## Evidence — Anterior vs. Conventional Approach

- In an **RCT, Liu and colleagues** found that the anterior approach for right hepatectomy had **beneficial effects on operative and survival outcomes** for patients with HCC
- However, **Ishizawa and associates** reported that:
  - The **conventional approach has the advantage** of preventing critical bleeding during liver transection
  - The **anterior approach is an effective alternative** when difficulty is encountered during liver mobilization
- **Further investigation is needed** to address this problem

## The Hanging Maneuver — Belghiti et al.

::: {.callout-note}
## Figure 120.8 — Hanging Maneuver
**(A)** A forceps is inserted **in front of the inferior vena cava (IVC)** from the **caudal side of the liver**; surgical tape is placed between the liver and the anterior surface of the IVC
**(B)** The tape is **lifted** to suspend the liver during division of the liver parenchyma
*(Belghiti J, et al. J Am Coll Surg. 2001;193:109–111)*
:::

## Advantages of the Hanging Maneuver

As an option to the anterior approach, this maneuver can:

- **Reduce blood loss** by compressing the liver parenchyma
- Make it **easier to determine the proper direction** of parenchymal division
- Allow **mobilization of the right liver to be avoided** during right hemihepatectomy, especially with a **large liver tumor**

## Applications and Risks of the Hanging Maneuver

- **Risk:** injury to the **short hepatic veins**
- Despite insufficient evidence, it is regarded as a **useful surgical technique**
- Widely applied to:
  - Liver transection for **left hepatectomy**
  - **Left caudate lobectomy**
  - **Laparoscopic liver resection**

---

## Hepatic Vein Reconstruction — Indication

- In liver resection for a malignant tumor, **hepatic venous reconstruction is also recommended** if the **functional volume of the residual liver is insufficient**

## Hepatic Vein Reconstruction — Technical Considerations

**Expansive growth type HCC:**

- Usually relatively **easy to detach** the HCC from the hepatic vein, even if closely attached

**Mixed or sclerosis type HCC:**

- Detachment may be **difficult because of tumor invasion**
- In such cases, **reconstruction techniques using an autologous vein graft** obtained from the resected liver specimen are useful

## Functional Implications of Congestion

- According to Kawaguchi and colleagues:
  - A **congestive area may be functional** to some degree
  - Corresponding to approximately **30%–40% of normal liver without congestion**
- These findings are being **investigated further**

---

## Conclusion

> **The safety and feasibility of liver resection for HCC are now established — even in patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension.**

This has been achieved by recent significant progress in:

- **Preoperative evaluation**
- **Surgical techniques**
- **Surgical devices**
- **Perioperative management**

## Key Takeaways — Indications

- **Makuuchi's criteria** (ascites, bilirubin, ICG R15) guide tolerable resection volume
- ICG R15 is the **most significant predictor of mortality**
- Portal hypertension increases risk but is **not an absolute contraindication** — surgical indications deserve further discussion
- BCLC guidelines **may need modification** regarding the role of surgery

## Key Takeaways — Perioperative Management

- **Spironolactone** routinely (100–200 mg/day based on ICG R15); furosemide for uncontrollable ascites
- Endoscopic evaluation and **prophylactic treatment of varices** (EVL/EIS/BRTO)
- **Splenectomy** for thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism

## Key Takeaways — Techniques

- **Intermittent Pringle maneuver** is the standard inflow occlusion
- **IOUS** is indispensable — including contrast-enhanced (Sonazoid)
- **Anatomic resection** is the procedure of choice when liver function allows
- ICG **fluorescence imaging** enables real-time segmental mapping
- Devices: **clamp crushing (standard), CUSA, vessel-sealing systems, vascular staplers**

## Key Takeaways — Approaches

- **Laparoscopic resection** offers particular benefits in cirrhosis (less ascites, shorter stay)
- **Anterior approach** — beneficial for large tumors; conventional approach retains advantage in bleeding control
- **Hanging maneuver** — reduces blood loss and guides transection direction
- **Hepatic vein reconstruction** preserves functional remnant volume
